subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Base Rate Neglect
description: A micro-lesson that makes Base Rate Neglect usable.

hook.text: A test is 99% accurate. You test positive. Most people assume 99% chance they're sick. They're wrong.

buildup.text: If the disease affects 1 in 10,000, most positives are false. The base rate matters enormously.

discovery.text: Base rate neglect: we focus on vivid details and ignore how common the condition really is.

twist.text: With a 1/10,000 base rate and 99% accuracy, your actual chance of being sick is under 1%.

climax.text: Before trusting a result, ask: how common is this in the population? The base rate changes everything.

quiz.question: What do people ignore in base rate neglect?
options: How common the condition is in the population

details.summary: Base rate neglect occurs when people ignore the underlying statistical frequency of an event and focus instead on specific case information. A positive test result feels alarming regardless of whether the condition affects one in ten or one in ten thousand people.
details.whyItMatters: Base rate neglect leads to dramatically wrong probability judgments in medicine, law, and finance. Without considering how common something is overall, specific evidence is systematically overweighted and overall probabilities are ignored.
takeaways: People overweight specific case information and underweight statistical base rates
Rare events with vivid cases seem more probable than they actually are
Bayesian reasoning corrects base rate neglect but feels unnatural

faq.question: What is a common example of base rate neglect?
faq.answer: A medical test with 95 percent accuracy sounds reliable. But if the disease affects only 1 in 1000 people, most positive results are false positives. People focus on the 95 percent accuracy and ignore the 0.1 percent base rate.

faq.question: How can base rate neglect be reduced in decision-making?
faq.answer: Using natural frequencies instead of percentages helps. Saying '1 out of 100 tested positive' is easier to process than '1 percent probability.' Visual representations and explicit base rate information before case details also help.
